description: A passionate team for curious minds.
summary:
TerraPulse is an interactive atlas that uses NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations to investigate how landscapes change. It follows four study areas: the Jamuna River and Tanguar Haor in Bangladesh, and Kathmandu and Rasuwa–Nuwakot in Nepal.

For NASA Space Apps’ Dancing with the SARs challenge, we developed a way to compare recorded radar visits on the same patch of ground. Users can swipe between dates, see whether a change persisted, and explore how differences in radar viewing geometry affect what the satellite can see. They can also find nearby NASA water or vegetation maps, check when those maps were acquired, and export an evidence dossier for someone else to review.

A dark patch in a radar image can have several explanations. By showing when it appeared, whether it persisted, and what other observations are available, TerraPulse helps field teams and researchers decide where to look next and what to verify on the ground.
details:
TerraPulse is an interactive atlas for investigating surface change with NASA–ISRO NISAR radar. We built it around four study areas. In Bangladesh, River Memory follows recurring radar signatures along the Jamuna River, while Wetland Pulse explores how radar returns change across Tanguar Haor. In Nepal, the Kathmandu investigation tracks whether a radar change persists, and the Rasuwa–Nuwakot investigation compares how consistently the radar signal matches across pairs of visits.

Users can play recorded visits, swipe between a selected date and a fixed reference, and compare two radar channels over the same footprint. Comparing both the previous visit and the fixed reference reveals changes that a single before-and-after view can miss. In one Kathmandu footprint, the HH radar return increased by 0.45 dB from the previous visit while remaining 7.08 dB below the reference. Users can export a dossier with the dates, footprint, measurements, and sources so another person can review the same evidence.

For the Dancing with the SARs challenge, we built a sensor lab where users can change the radar viewing angle and direction over 3D terrain to see how slopes create shadow and layover. A second lab lets them vary soil moisture, standing water, and vegetation, then compare the modeled radar response with a recorded NISAR visit. The Atlas also links to dated NASA OPERA water and vegetation disturbance maps so users can check whether a pattern appears in another satellite record.

We used Python, with h5py, NumPy, and Rasterio, to read satellite files and prepare aligned map layers and measurements. We built the Atlas with JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and Canvas and used NASADEM for terrain. The judging edition runs in a standard browser with prepared assets, so reviewers can explore it without specialist hardware or large satellite downloads.

Our team considered acquisition gaps, differences in sensor geometry, the timing and coverage of comparison maps, and the risk of assigning a physical cause from radar alone. TerraPulse keeps observations, simulations, and supporting evidence clearly labeled. Its intended impact is to help researchers and field teams identify where to investigate next and what evidence to collect, while giving students a hands-on way to learn how radar sees the Earth.
